headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Dietary Supplements
headings.content: A dietary supplement is a manufactured product intended to supplement one's diet by taking a pill, capsule, tablet, powder, or liquid. These products can provide nutrients either extracted from food sources or synthesized in a laboratory to increase the consumption of their quantity. The class of dietary products includes vitamins, minerals, herbs, amino acids, and enzymes. Unlike conventional foods, supplements are not meant to be a primary source of nourishment or a sole meal replacement. Nurses must understand that while these products aim to boost nutritional intake, they cannot substitute for a balanced, whole-food diet.

headings.title: Regulatory Framework and Safety Standards in Nigeria
headings.content: In Nigeria, the regulation and control of dietary supplements fall primarily under the mandate of the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC). Manufacturers must register their products and prove safety before public sale. However, the market still sees many unregistered or falsely labeled products circulating through open-air drug markets. Nurses play a crucial role in protecting patients by advising them to check for valid NAFDAC registration numbers on product labels before purchasing or consuming any health supplement.

headings.title: Common Types of Dietary Supplements and Their Purposes
headings.content:
- **Vitamins**: Organic compounds like Vitamin C and B-complex needed in small quantities for vital metabolic functions.
- **Minerals**: Inorganic elements such as iron, calcium, and zinc required for structural support and enzymatic reactions.
- **Herbal products**: Plant-derived preparations, including garlic, ginger, and bitter leaf extracts, used traditionally for health maintenance.
- **Protein powders**: Concentrated amino acid sources commonly utilized by athletes to build muscle mass.

headings.title: Nutrient Deficiencies and High-Risk Populations
headings.content: Certain groups in the population face a much higher risk of developing vitamin and mineral deficiencies due to increased physiological demands or restricted dietary intake. Pregnant women require extra folic acid and iron to support fetal development and prevent neural tube defects. Infants, the elderly, and individuals living with chronic malabsorptive disorders often need targeted supplementation. A common clinical mistake is assuming every fatigued patient needs a general multivitamin without first checking laboratory blood values to identify the exact root deficiency.

headings.title: Potential Risks, Toxicity, and Adverse Drug Interactions
headings.content: Natural does not automatically mean safe. Fat-soluble vitamins like Vitamin A, D, E, and K can accumulate in the body's fatty tissues and liver, leading to dangerous toxicity over time. Herbal supplements frequently interact with orthodox medications. For instance, St. John's Wort can speed up the breakdown of many prescription drugs, reducing their effectiveness. Furthermore, garlic and ginkgo biloba supplements can increase the risk of bleeding when taken alongside blood thinners like warfarin or aspirin.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Patient History Taking
headings.content: During admission and routine clinic visits, nurses must ask patients specifically about any supplements, herbs, or traditional remedies they take. Many patients omit this information because they view supplements as harmless food items rather than active medications. The nursing assessment should cover the name of the product, dosage, frequency, reason for use, and where the item was purchased. Uncovering this history helps prevent unexpected adverse drug reactions while the patient is admitted to the ward.

headings.title: Dietary Counselling and Patient Education Strategies
headings.content: Effective patient education bridges the gap between traditional practices and safe clinical care. Nurses should use simple, non-judgmental language when discussing supplements with patients. Education must focus on realistic dosing, potential side effects, and the importance of purchasing only NAFDAC-approved products. Nurses should also advise patients to bring all their supplement bottles to follow-up appointments so the clinical team can review them together.
